reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A fibroblastic tumour of intermediate behaviour that can arise almost anywhere, historically described in the pleura but common in extrapleural soft tissue
Usually a slow-growing, well-circumscribed mass; deep-seated lesions may reach a large size before detection
Defined molecularly by a recurrent NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, which produces diffuse nuclear STAT6 expression on immunohistochemistry
Histology shows a patternless architecture of bland spindle cells, ropey collagen and branching staghorn-shaped thin-walled vessels
The term haemangiopericytoma is now regarded as part of the solitary fibrous tumour spectrum
A minority secrete insulin-like growth factor and cause hypoglycaemia, known as Doege-Potter syndrome
Complete surgical excision is the mainstay of treatment, with long-term follow-up because late recurrence and metastasis can occur
reference.pathophysiology: Solitary fibrous tumour is a fibroblastic neoplasm defined by an intrachromosomal NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion arising from an inversion on chromosome 12. This fusion converts the normally repressive NAB2 into a transcriptional activator of EGR1 target genes, driving cell proliferation, and results in nuclear relocation of STAT6 that can be detected immunohistochemically. The tumour is composed of a haphazard arrangement of bland ovoid to spindled cells set in variably collagenous stroma with characteristic dilated, branching thin-walled vessels. Although most behave in an indolent fashion, a subset shows malignant features and can metastasise, so behaviour is stratified using mitotic activity, size, necrosis and age.
additionalDifferentials: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour in abdominal sites
additionalInvestigations: MRI or CT to define the well-circumscribed mass and its vascularity
Core biopsy with histological assessment of the patternless pattern and staghorn vessels
STAT6 immunohistochemistry as a highly specific diagnostic marker
Molecular confirmation of the NAB2-STAT6 fusion in uncertain cases
Blood glucose evaluation if symptoms suggest tumour-related hypoglycaemia
redFlags: Large size, high mitotic count or necrosis indicating a malignant solitary fibrous tumour
Rapid growth or evidence of distant spread on staging
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia suggesting a functioning tumour
Late local recurrence or metastasis during follow-up
reference.prognosis: Most solitary fibrous tumours are cured by complete excision, but the entity has intermediate malignant potential, and a subset recurs or metastasises, sometimes many years later. Risk stratification using size, mitoses, necrosis and age guides surveillance intensity.
pitfalls: Assuming all solitary fibrous tumours are benign and omitting long-term follow-up
Confusing it with synovial sarcoma or other spindle-cell tumours without STAT6 testing
Overlooking tumour-associated hypoglycaemia as a paraneoplastic clue
Relying on morphology alone when the molecular signature clarifies the diagnosis
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Complete wide surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay and offers cure for localised disease
Refer to a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team for surgical planning and pathological risk stratification by size, mitoses, necrosis and age
Adjuvant or salvage radiotherapy for incompletely resected, recurrent or high-risk tumours
Antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as pazopanib or sunitinib for unresectable or metastatic disease
Correct tumour-related (Doege-Potter) hypoglycaemia with dextrose and glucocorticoids, with resection being definitive
Prolonged, risk-stratified surveillance imaging because local recurrence and metastasis may appear many years later
